newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian economic problems remain after IMF handout.
newsitem.headline: Russian economic problems remain after IMF handout.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund's decision to hand over almost $650 million of its $10 billion three-year loan to Russia is a vote of confidence in Moscow's painful economic reforms.
But Russia's finance ministers, their economy still shaky after a five-year slump, have plenty to worry about.

Tax evasion and other non-payments threaten government spending plans, parliament has not yet passed a much-needed tax code and a report released last month says official unemployment figures mask a much more serious state of affairs.

"There is a problem on taxes and they should carry out tax reform," German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said Saturday during a meeting of Western financial leaders, adding that reforms were needed to allow a market economy to take shape.
But Waigel, speaking in Berlin, also said the Russian economy was developing satisfactorily.

That development brought Russia a tentative sign of economic growth last month, when industrial output crept 0.3 percent above year-ago levels and gross domestic product rose a meagre 0.1 percent. GDP fell six percent last year.

But output is still around half that when Russia launched its first economic reform programme in January 1992 and companies have struggled to fulfil their Soviet-era obligations, including maintaining a social infrastructure.
Some ministers admit that last year was wasted for reform as the government concentrated on funding President Boris Yeltsin's re-election campaign.

"The Russian economy was sacrificed for Russian democracy last year," Economy Minister Yevgeny Yasin said this month. "We saw a fairly significant drop in output and a deterioration in our finances...we've ended up with a desperate budget crisis."
Yeltsin defeated a communist candidate in the July vote, but then disappeared, first with heart problems and then with pneumonia. Economic reforms were effectively put on hold.
The IMF, angered by abysmal tax revenues, withheld two tranches of its latest credit in the final quarter of last year, although it relented as tax money started flowing in.
This month's payment -- one delayed tranche and one regular one released last Friday -- is a sign that the IMF is happier than it was before.
"Russia's economic relations with the West are doing fine," Russian television's evening news programme said Saturday.
But official figurers show that tax arrears rose to 128.25 trillion roubles ($23 billion) at the start of this year, more than twice the level at the start of 1996.

A total of 1,665 companies each owed the state more than three billion roubles ($535,000) in back taxes and fines and more than 80 firms owed 100 billion roubles ($18 million), although December's debt was smaller than the November one.
The companies argue that they cannot afford to pay tax while they are owed money for deliveries.
The government, especially the military-industrial complex, is one of the biggest non-payers in a vicious circle of debt.
Firms often respond to the crisis by delaying wage payments, although few have sacked workers.
Unemployment is just under 10 percent, using Western methods, but a report last month by International Labour Organisation experts says it could be more than that.
"For the past five years unemployment in Russia has been chronically understated and is well over 10 percent," the report said.

The government wants monthly inflation below one percent this year, but prices rose 2.3 percent in January, up from 1.4 percent in December. Prices rose 4.1 percent in January 1996 and the month tends to have the highest inflation rate of the year.
